summary: Children aged 8–11 learn to compare multiple possible design solutions against one shared set of criteria and constraints, then select the most promising with reasoning that points at the evidence. The core skill is holding a single yardstick across at least three distinct options: rating each on each criterion, gating out any that break a must-meet constraint, and accepting that the best choice is often a trade-off rather than a winner on every row. Activities span building a working comparison matrix, defending a choice in dialogue, reading a worked matrix, and judging pre-filled comparisons — each targeting a different part of generate-compare-select.
misconceptions: Picking the first or best-liked idea instead of comparing several against the criteria.
Judging each solution on different, self-chosen strengths rather than one shared set of criteria.
Ignoring constraints — choosing a solution that scores well but breaks the budget or materials limit.
Believing the best solution must win on every criterion, rather than being the best overall trade-off.
Selecting without reasoning, or with reasoning ('it looks cool') unconnected to the criteria and evidence.

activities.title: Solution Showdown: build and reason across your own comparison matrix
steps: Start from a defined brief whose criteria and constraints are already set (e.g. a lunchbox insulator that keeps an ice cube frozen from morning to lunch, fits the box, uses only allowed materials, and stays under budget).
Invent at least three genuinely different candidate solutions and lay them out as side-by-side cards before judging any of them.
Rate each solution on every criterion by filling the cells of a shared solutions×criteria grid.
Apply a constraint gate: mark each solution pass/fail on each must-meet limit (materials, size, time, cost); any solution that breaks a constraint is eliminated regardless of its ratings.
Select the most promising solution and justify it by pointing at specific grid cells — e.g. 'B keeps the ice frozen longer and stays under budget where A fails' — naming the trade-off accepted.
Work through at least one case engineered so no option wins every row, so 'most promising overall' becomes the honest goal.
activities.insight: A defensible choice emerges from one yardstick applied to every option; a constraint is a gate that eliminates, not a preference to weigh, and the best solution is usually an explicit trade-off you can point to.

activities.title: Defend your choice to a design mentor
steps: Present three candidate solutions and an initial pick to a mentor (teacher, peer, or in-role character) who will not accept 'I like it' or 'it looks cool'.
Answer pressing questions that force reasoning across all three ideas: 'Compared to your other two ideas, why this one?' and 'Which criterion does each idea win or lose on?'

Respond to follow-ups that test the robustness of the choice: 'Which of the other two came closest, and what ruled it out?', 'If the budget doubled, would you still choose this?', 'If it had to stay frozen until home time, would your choice change?'
activities.insight: A choice is only justified when it is argued against the alternatives on the shared criteria and constraints; impulse picks collapse under 'which criterion does it win on?'

activities.title: Read a worked comparison matrix
steps: Study an annotated decision matrix comparing several solutions across the same criteria.
Reveal, cell by cell, why each solution rates as it does on each criterion.
Reveal the reasoning behind the chosen winner, including where the trade-off lies and which rows it loses.
activities.insight: A good comparison applies the same criteria to every option and names the trade-off behind the winner; this is what a defensible selection looks like before you build your own.

activities.title: Judge pre-filled comparisons
steps: Given a completed solutions×criteria matrix, choose the most promising solution and state why in terms of the rows.
Sort candidate options into 'meets constraints' and 'eliminated' categories.
Rank the solutions that remain after setting aside any that fail a must-meet constraint by overall fit against the criteria.
Complete a 'chosen because…' justification that references specific rows of the matrix.
activities.insight: Drawing the right conclusion from a comparison means reading across shared criteria, gating constraint-breakers first, and tying the choice to named rows.

checkQuestion: Here is the problem: design a lunchbox insulator that keeps an ice cube frozen from morning until lunch. It must fit inside this lunchbox, use only the materials on the table, and cost no more than the budget on the card. Come up with three different possible designs, then decide which one you'd build — talk me through why as you go. (Set the task, provide the materials/criteria/constraint card, and watch what the child does; do not explain how to compare.)
checkAnswer: The child generates three genuinely different solutions, weighs each explicitly against the stated criteria (keeps ice frozen, fits the box) and constraints (allowed materials, budget), and selects one with reasons that refer back to those criteria and constraints — e.g. 'this one traps the most air so it insulates best and still fits, and it's under budget'.
